props.title: Wild Wild West

sections.content: **Wild Wild West** (1999) represents one of Hollywood's most notorious big-budget misfires, taking a beloved 1960s TV series and transforming it into a steampunk spectacle that prioritized mechanical spiders over coherent storytelling. Will Smith, fresh off the success of **Men in Black** (1997), reunited with director Barry Sonnenfeld, but lightning didn't strike twice. The film's troubled production and $170 million budget resulted in a box office bomb that effectively killed the steampunk Western genre before it could gain traction, unlike successful genre hybrids like **Back to the Future Part III** (1990).

sections.content: The failure of **Wild Wild West** (1999) highlighted Hollywood's challenging relationship with the Western genre in the modern era. While pure Westerns like **Unforgiven** (1992) and **Open Range** (2003) found success by embracing traditional themes, attempts to modernize the genre through sci-fi and fantasy elements repeatedly stumbled. **The Adventures of Brisco County Jr.** (1993) on television managed to blend steampunk and Western elements successfully, but theatrical releases consistently missed the mark. SUBHEAD: The Impact on Will Smith's Career

The film marked a rare misstep in Will Smith's meteoric rise during the 1990s. After string of hits including **Independence Day** (1996) and **Enemy of the State** (1998), **Wild Wild West** (1999) became his first major failure. Smith later expressed regret about choosing the film over the role of Neo in **The Matrix** (1999), making it one of Hollywood's most famous casting "what-ifs." However, he quickly rebounded with dramatic roles in **Ali** (2001) and **I Am Legend** (2007).
